paragraphs.text: The concept of money as a means of exchange, a means to store wealth or make payments goes back at least as far as the first written sources of the third millennium BC. Ingots of precious metal, silver in particular, had been used in trade all over the Mediterranean world well before coins. The invention of coinage in the second half of the seventh century BC produced a commodity that no longer needed to be weighed for every transaction, provided it was made of precious metal, was adjusted to a specific weight standard, and bore the mark or stamp of the issuing authority , guaranteeing its legal tender.
How were coins manufactured in ancient Greece?

Coins were made from precious metals at what was known as a mint. Very little remains of the actual buildings, though we do know where the mint was in ancient Athens. Even less is known from ancient literary sources, so our knowledge is mainly empirical, based on examination of the surviving coins themselves. Most ancient coins were made on an anvil by hand from a pair of stamps known as dies. The dies were engraved by hand. One die was fixed in the anvil and was called the obverse die. The other, called the reverse die, was held loosely. A blank lump of metal, the flan, was inserted between the two, and the pile of three items, known as the stack, was struck with a hammer. The result of the blow was the coin. Bronze coins were sometimes cast in clay or stone molds, an experimental manufacturing technique used at the beginning of Greek bronze coinage in the fifth century BC. It was also used at the beginning of Roman bronze coinage in the third century BC, mainly for coins that were too large to be struck, but the process soon proved to be cumbersome and tended to produce results of poorer quality.
How did coinage spread throughout the ancient world?

Coinage most likely began in western Asia Minor. The earliest coins were discovered in the excavations of Ephesus in lonia. They were made of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver found in the River Pactolos in Lydia. Current evidence indicates that coinage was introduced by the early kings of Lydia. King Croesus, who ruled Lydia from 560 to 546 BC, replaced electrum coinage with a bimetallic system based on gold and silver. The earlier variety of coin types and denominations —from the largest, a full stater of about 12-17g, through numerous fractions of a stater to the smallest, a ninety-sixth of a stater of about 0.15g — was unified into a single gold stater and a silver siglos, with foreparts of a lion and a bull confronted on the obverse. When the Persians under Cyrus the Great conquered Lydia in 547-546 BC, they adopted the use of the coinage they found and this continued until the reign of Darius I who introduced his own gold coin, the daric and a new siglos, with the king shown on it.

One could argue about how Greek the Lydians were, but if coinage is considered a Greek invention, the reason is that in the second half of the sixth through to the fifth century BC, the use of coins spread very rapidly into the Greek world, the rest of Asia Minor and the islands, and was adopted in mainland Greece and Sicily. Coins of these regions were usually made of silver, extracted from the mines on some of the islands. The earliest major mint in Greece was probably on Aegina, the small island across from the Athens, famous for its seafaring trade, followed by Athens and Corinth from about 550BC on. All three mints used different weight standards. Athens became the most important mint in the fifth century BC and the only one to issue a truly international currency before Alexander the Great. These silver tetradrachms, known popularly as 'owls', circulated everywhere in the Greek world and were accepted because of their recognized value and fineness.

Every Greek city-state, or polis, could issue its own currency and the development of such independent coinages arguably can be associated with, if not attributed to, the development of Greek democracy. Indeed, one of the reasons for the introduction of coinage may have been the need for a more equitable distribution of wealth and a more measurable means of remuneration for workers at all levels of Greek society.

Coins are original contemporary objects, unlike the writings of the ancient historians, transmitted to us through a series of later authors or transcriptions, or the great masterpieces of classical sculpture, known mainly through Roman copies from the lost bronze originals. Coins are invaluable historical documents that can shed light on the past of a little-known city, its cults and its art. In excavations, they can help date the archeological context. Coins attest to the extent of various rulers' territories or other aspects of trade such as the routes taken. They were ideal vehicles of political propaganda, and they often advertised the virtues and exploits of kings and emperors. In spite of their small size, coins of high quality reflect the esthetic and artistic values of their time with the immediacy of true masterpieces.
